## 13.2 Change of Basis

Suppose we have two ordered bases $S=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})$ and $S^{\prime}=(v_{1}^{\prime},\dots,v_{n}^{\prime})$ for a vector space $V.$ （Here $v_{i}$ and $v_{i}^{\prime}$ are vectors, not components of vectors in a basis!) Then we may write each $v_{k}^{\prime}$ uniquely as

$$
v _ {k} ^ {\prime} = \sum_ {i} v _ {i} p _ {k} ^ {i},
$$

this is $v_{k}^{\prime}$ as a linear combination of the $v_{i}.$ In matrix notation
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
$$
v _ {k} ^ {\prime} = \sum_ {i} v _ {i} p _ {k} ^ {i},
$$

this is $v_{k}^{\prime}$ as a linear combination of the $v_{i}.$ In matrix notation

$$
\left(v _ {1} ^ {\prime}, v _ {2} ^ {\prime}, \dots , v _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(v _ {1}, v _ {2}, \dots , v _ {n}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} p _ {1} ^ {1} & p _ {2} ^ {1} & \dots & p _ {n} ^ {1} \\ p _ {1} ^ {2} & p _ {2} ^ {2} & & \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ p _ {1} ^ {n} & & \dots & p _ {n} ^ {n} \end{array} \right).
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Here, the $p_{k}^{i}$ are constants, which we can regard as entries of a square matrix $P=(p_{k}^{i})$ . The matrix P must have an inverse since we can also write each $v_{j}$ uniquely as a linear combination of the $v_{k}^{\prime}$

$$
v _ {j} = \sum_ {k} v _ {k} ^ {\prime} q _ {j} ^ {k}.
$$

Then we can write

$$
v _ {j} = \sum_ {k} \sum_ {i} v _ {i} p _ {k} ^ {i} q _ {j} ^ {k}.
$$

But $\sum_{k} p_{k}^{i} q_{j}^{k}$ is the k,j entry of the product matrix PQ. Since the expression for $v_{j}$ in the basis S is $v_{j}$ itself, then PQ maps each $v_{j}$ to itself. As a result, each $v_{j}$ is an eigenvector for PQ with eigenvalue 1, so PQ is the identity, i.e.

$$
P Q = I \Leftrightarrow Q = P ^ {- 1}.
$$

The matrix $P$ is called a change of basis matrix. There is a quick and dirty trick to obtain it; look at the formula above relating the new basis vectors $v_{1}^{\prime},v_{2}^{\prime},\ldots v_{n}^{\prime}$ to the old ones $v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}$ . In particular focus on $v_{1}^{\prime}$ for which

$$
v _ {1} ^ {\prime} = \left(v _ {1}, v _ {2}, \dots , v _ {n}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c} p _ {1} ^ {1} \\ p _ {1} ^ {2} \\ \vdots \\ p _ {1} ^ {n} \end{array} \right).
$$

This says that the first column of the change of basis matrix P is really just the components of the vector $v_{1}^{\prime}$ in the basis $v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}.$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
This says that the first column of the change of basis matrix P is really just the components of the vector $v_{1}^{\prime}$ in the basis $v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}.$

The columns of the change of basis matrix are the components of the new basis vectors in terms of the old basis vectors.

Example 130 Suppose $S^{\prime}=\left(v_{1}^{\prime},v_{2}^{\prime}\right)$ is an ordered basis for a vector space V and that with respect to some other ordered basis $S=\left(v_{1},v_{2}\right)$ for V

$$
v _ {1} ^ {\prime} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right) _ {S} \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad v _ {2} ^ {\prime} = \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ - \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \end{array} \right) _ {S}.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
This means

$$
v _ {1} ^ {\prime} = \left(v _ {1}, v _ {2}\right) \binom {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}} {\frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}} = \frac {v _ {1} + v _ {2}}{\sqrt {2}} \quad \mathrm {a n d} \quad v _ {2} ^ {\prime} = \left(v _ {1}, v _ {2}\right) \binom {\frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}} {- \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}}} = \frac {v _ {1} - v _ {2}}{\sqrt {3}}.
$$

The change of basis matrix has as its columns just the components of $v_{1}^{\prime}$ and $v_{2}^{\prime};$

$$
P = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & - \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \end{array} \right).
$$

Changing basis changes the matrix of a linear transformation. However, as a map between vector spaces, the linear transformation is the same no matter which basis we use. Linear transformations are the actual objects of study of this book, not matrices; matrices are merely a convenient way of doing computations.

Change of Basis Example

Lets now calculate how the matrix of a linear transformation changes when changing basis. To wit, let $L\colon V\longrightarrow W$ with matrix $M=(m_{j}^{i})$ in the ordered input and output bases $S=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})$ and $T=(w_{1},\dots,w_{m})$ so

$$
L \left(v _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {k} w _ {k} m _ {i} ^ {k}.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
$$
L \left(v _ {i}\right) = \sum_ {k} w _ {k} m _ {i} ^ {k}.
$$

Now, suppose $S^{\prime}=\left(v_{1}^{\prime},\dots,v_{n}^{\prime}\right)$ and $T^{\prime}=\left(w_{1}^{\prime},\dots,w_{m}^{\prime}\right)$ are new ordered input and out bases with matrix $M^{\prime}=\left(m_{i}^{\prime k}\right).$ Then

$$
L \left(v _ {i} ^ {\prime}\right) = \sum_ {k} w _ {k} m _ {i} ^ {\prime k}.
$$

Let $P=(p_{j}^{i})$ be the change of basis matrix from input basis S to the basis $S^{\prime}$ and $Q=(q_{k}^{j})$ be the change of basis matrix from output basis T to the basis $T^{\prime}$ . Then:

$$
L \left(v _ {j} ^ {\prime}\right) = L \left(\sum_ {i} v _ {i} p _ {j} ^ {i}\right) = \sum_ {i} L \left(v _ {i}\right) p _ {j} ^ {i} = \sum_ {i} \sum_ {k} w _ {k} m _ {i} ^ {k} p _ {j} ^ {i}.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Meanwhile, we have:

$$
L \left(v _ {i} ^ {\prime}\right) = \sum_ {k} v _ {k} m _ {i} ^ {\prime k} = \sum_ {k} \sum_ {j} v _ {j} q _ {k} ^ {j} m _ {i} ^ {k}.
$$

Since the expression for a vector in a basis is unique, then we see that the entries of MP are the same as the entries of $Q M^{\prime}$ . In other words, we see that

$$
M P = Q M ^ {\prime} \quad \mathrm {o r} \quad M ^ {\prime} = Q ^ {- 1} M P.
$$

Example 131 Let V be the space of polynomials in t and degree 2 or less and $L:V\to \mathbb{R}^{2}$ where

$$
L (1) = \binom {1} {2} \quad L (t) = \binom {2} {1}, \quad L \left(t ^ {2}\right) = \binom {3} {3}.
$$

From this information we can immediately read off the matrix M of L in the bases $S=(1,t, t^{2})$ and $T=(e_{1}, e_{2})$ , the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , because

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(L (1), L (t), L \left(t ^ {2}\right)\right) = \left(e _ {1} + 2 e _ {2}, 2 e _ {1} + e _ {2}, 3 e _ {1} + 3 e _ {2}\right) \\ = \left(e _ {1}, e _ {2}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right) \Rightarrow M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$

Now suppose we are more interested in the bases
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Now suppose we are more interested in the bases

$$
S ^ {\prime} = \left(1 + t, t + t ^ {2}, 1 + t ^ {2}\right), \quad T ^ {\prime} = \left(\binom {1} {2}, \binom {2} {1}\right) =: \left(w _ {1} ^ {\prime}, w _ {2} ^ {\prime}\right).
$$

To compute the new matrix $M^{\prime}$ of L we could simply calculate what L does the the new input basis vectors in terms of the new output basis vectors:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(L (1 + t), L \left(t + t ^ {2}\right), L \left(1 + t ^ {2}\right)\right) = \left(\binom {1} {2} + \binom {2} {1}, \binom {2} {1} + \binom {3} {3}, \binom {1} {2} + \binom {3} {3}\right) \\ = \left(w _ {1} ^ {\prime} + w _ {2} ^ {\prime}, w _ {1} ^ {\prime} + 2 w _ {2} ^ {\prime}, 2 w _ {1} ^ {\prime} + w _ {2} ^ {\prime}\right) \\ = \left(w _ {1} ^ {\prime}, w _ {2} ^ {\prime}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array} \right) \Rightarrow M ^ {\prime} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$

Alternatively we could calculate the change of basis matrices P and Q by noting that

Alternatively we could calculate the change of basis matrices P and Q by noting that

$$
(1 + t, t + t ^ {2}, 1 + t ^ {2}) = (1, t, t ^ {2}) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \right) \Rightarrow P = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \right)
$$

and

$$
\left(w _ {1} ^ {\prime}, w _ {2} ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(e _ {1} + 2 e _ {2}, 2 e _ {1} + e _ {2}\right) = \left(e _ {1}, e _ {1}\right) \binom {1} {2} \Rightarrow Q = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{array} \right).
$$

Hence

$$
M ^ {\prime} = Q ^ {- 1} M P = - \frac {1}{3} \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & - 2 \\ - 2 & 1 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{array} \right).

Notice that the change of basis matrices P and Q are both square and invertible. Also, since we really wanted $Q^{-1}$ , it is more efficient to try and write $(e_{1}, e_{2})$ in terms of $(w_{1}^{\prime}, w_{2}^{\prime})$ which would yield directly $Q^{-1}$ . Alternatively, one can check that $MP=QM^{\prime}.$

## 13.3 Changing to a Basis of Eigenvectors

If we are changing to a basis of eigenvectors, then there are various simplifications:

- Since $L : V \to V$ , most likely you already know the matrix M of L using the same input basis as output basis $S=(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})$ (say).
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
- Since $L : V \to V$ , most likely you already know the matrix M of L using the same input basis as output basis $S=(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})$ (say).

- In the new basis of eigenvectors $S^{\prime}(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})$ , the matrix D of L is diagonal because $L v_{i}=\lambda_{i} v_{i}$ and so

$$
\left(L \left(v _ {1}\right), L \left(v _ {2}\right), \dots , L \left(v _ {n}\right)\right) = \left(v _ {1}, v _ {2}, \dots , v _ {n}\right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} \lambda_ {1} & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_ {2} & & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & \lambda_ {n} \end{array} \right).
$$

- If P is the change of basis matrix from S to $S^{\prime}$ , the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues D and the original matrix are related by

$$
D = P ^ {- 1} M P
$$

This motivates the following definition:
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Definition A matrix M is diagonalizable if there exists an invertible matrix P and a diagonal matrix D such that

$$
D = P ^ {- 1} M P.
$$

We can summarize as follows.

- Change of basis rearranges the components of a vector by the change of basis matrix P, to give components in the new basis.

- To get the matrix of a linear transformation in the new basis, we conjugate the matrix of L by the change of basis matrix: $M\mapsto P^{-1}MP.$

If for two matrices N and M there exists a matrix P such that $M=P^{-1} N P$ , then we say that M and N are similar. Then the above discussion shows that diagonalizable matrices are similar to diagonal matrices.

Corollary 13.3.1. A square matrix M is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of eigenvectors for M. Moreover, these eigenvectors are the columns of a change of basis matrix P which diagonalizes M.

Example 132 Let's try to diagonalize the matrix

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} - 1 4 & - 2 8 & - 4 4 \\ - 7 & - 1 4 & - 2 3 \\ 9 & 1 8 & 2 9 \end{array} \right).
$$

The eigenvalues of M are determined by

$$
\det (M - \lambda I) = - \lambda^ {3} + \lambda^ {2} + 2 \lambda = 0.
$$

So the eigenvalues of M are $- 1,0$ , and 2, and associated eigenvectors turn out to be

$$
v _ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c} - 8 \\ - 1 \\ 3 \end{array} \right), v _ {2} = \left( \begin{array}{c} - 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \text {a n d} v _ {3} = \left( \begin{array}{c} - 1 \\ - 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right).
$$

$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

# Orthonormal Bases and Complements

You may have noticed that we have only rarely used the dot product. That is because many of the results we have obtained do not require a preferred notion of lengths of vectors. Once a dot or inner product is available, lengths of and angles between vectors can be measured-very powerful machinery and results are available in this case.

## 14.1 Properties of the Standard Basis

The standard notion of the length of a vector $x = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \dots, x_{n}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is

$$
| | x | | = \sqrt {x \cdot x} = \sqrt {\left(x _ {1}\right) ^ {2} + \left(x _ {2}\right) ^ {2} + \cdots \left(x _ {n}\right) ^ {2}}.
$$

The canonical/standard basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

$$
e _ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \quad e _ {2} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \quad \dots , \quad e _ {n} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{array} \right),
$$

has many useful properties with respect to the dot product and lengths.

Each of the standard basis vectors has unit length;

$$
\left\| e _ {i} \right\| = \sqrt {e _ {i} \cdot e _ {i}} = \sqrt {e _ {i} ^ {T} e _ {i}} = 1.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
- The standard basis vectors are orthogonal (in other words, at right angles or perpendicular);

$$
e _ {i} \cdot e _ {j} = e _ {i} ^ {T} e _ {j} = 0 \mathrm {w h e n} i \neq j
$$

This is summarized by

$$
e _ {i} ^ {T} e _ {j} = \delta_ {i j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \neq j \end{array} , \right.
$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. Notice that the Kronecker delta gives the entries of the identity matrix.

Given column vectors $v$ and $w$ , we have seen that the dot product $v\cdot w$ is the same as the matrix multiplication $v^{T}w$ . This is an inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ We can also form the outer product $v w^{T}$ , which gives a square matrix. The outer product on the standard basis vectors is interesting. Set

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Pi_ {1} = e _ {1} e _ {1} ^ {T} \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \end{array} \right) \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 \end{array} \right) \\ \end{array}
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?
What is Linear Algebra?

text:
In short, $\Pi_{i}$ is the diagonal square matrix with a 1 in the i'th diagonal position and zeros everywhere else $^{1}$

Notice that $\Pi_{i}\Pi_{j}=e_{i}e_{i}^{T}e_{j}e_{j}^{T}=e_{i}\delta_{ij}e_{j}^{T}.$ Then:

$$
\Pi_ {i} \Pi_ {j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{c c c} \Pi_ {i} & i = j \\ 0 & i \neq j \end{array} . \right.
$$

Moreover, for a diagonal matrix D with diagonal entries $\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}$ , we can write

$$
D = \lambda_ {1} \Pi_ {1} + \dots + \lambda_ {n} \Pi_ {n}.
$$

## 14.2 Orthogonal and Orthonormal Bases

There are many other bases that behave in the same way as the standard basis. As such, we will study:

- Orthogonal bases $\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}$:

$$
v _ {i} \cdot v _ {j} = 0 \mathrm {i f} i \neq j.
$$

In other words, all vectors in the basis are perpendicular.

- Orthonormal bases { $u_{1}, \dots, u_{n}$ }:

$$
u _ {i} \cdot u _ {j} = \delta_ {i j}.
$$

In addition to being orthogonal, each vector has unit length.

Suppose $T=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{n}.$ Because T is a basis, we can write any vector v uniquely as a linear combination of the vectors in T;

$$
v = c ^ {1} u _ {1} + \dots c ^ {n} u _ {n}.
$$

Since T is orthonormal, there is a very easy way to find the coefficients of this linear combination. By taking the dot product of v with any of the vectors

$^{1}$ This is reminiscent of an older notation, where vectors are written in juxtaposition. This is called a "dyadic tensor", and is still used in some applications.
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
in T, we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} v \cdot u _ {i} = c ^ {1} u _ {1} \cdot u _ {i} + \dots + c ^ {i} u _ {i} \cdot u _ {i} + \dots + c ^ {n} u _ {n} \cdot u _ {i} \\ = c ^ {1} \cdot 0 + \dots + c ^ {i} \cdot 1 + \dots + c ^ {n} \cdot 0 \\ = c ^ {i}, \\ \Rightarrow c ^ {i} = v \cdot u _ {i} \\ \Rightarrow v = (v \cdot u _ {1}) u _ {1} + \dots + (v \cdot u _ {n}) u _ {n} \\ = \sum_ {i} (v \cdot u _ {i}) u _ {i}. \\ \end{array}
$$

This proves the following theorem.

Theorem 14.2.1. For an orthonormal basis $\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\}$ any vector v can be expressed as

$$
v = \sum_ {i} \left(v \cdot u _ {i}\right) u _ {i}.
$$

## 14.2.1 Orthonormal Bases and Dot Products

To calculate lengths of, and angles between vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ we most commonly use the dot product:

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c} v ^ {1} \\ \vdots \\ v ^ {n} \end{array} \right) \cdot \left( \begin{array}{c} w ^ {1} \\ \vdots \\ w ^ {n} \end{array} \right) := v ^ {1} w ^ {1} + \dots + v ^ {n} w ^ {n}.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
When dealing with more general vector spaces the dot product makes no sense, and one must instead choose an appropriate inner product. By "appropriate", we mean an inner product well-suited to the problem one is trying to solve. If the vector space V under study has an orthonormal basis $O=(u_{1},\dots,u_{n})$ meaning

$$
\langle u _ {i}, u _ {j} \rangle = \delta_ {i j},
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product, you might ask whether this can be related to a dot product? The answer to this question is yes and rather easy to understand:

Given an orthonormal basis, the information of two vectors $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ in V can be encoded in column vectors

$$
v = \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle u _ {1} + \dots + \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle u _ {n} = \left(u _ {1}, \dots , u _ {n}\right) \binom {\langle v, u _ {1} \rangle} {\vdots} = \binom {\langle v, u _ {1} \rangle} {\vdots} _ {O},
$$

$$
v ^ {\prime} = \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle u _ {1} + \dots + \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle u _ {n} = \left(u _ {1}, \dots , u _ {n}\right) \binom {\langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle} {\vdots} = \binom {\langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle} {\vdots} _ {O}.
$$

The dot product of these two column vectors is

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c} \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle \\ \vdots \\ \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle \end{array} \right) \cdot \left( \begin{array}{c} \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle \\ \vdots \\ \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle \end{array} \right) = \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle + \dots + \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle .
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
This agrees exactly with the inner product of $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ because

$$
\begin{array}{l} \langle v, v ^ {\prime} \rangle = \left\langle \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle u _ {1} + \dots + \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle u _ {n}, \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle u _ {1} + \dots + \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle u _ {n} \right\rangle \\ = \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle \langle u _ {1}, u _ {1} \rangle + \langle v, u _ {2} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle \langle u _ {2}, u _ {1} \rangle + \dots \\ \dots + \langle v, u _ {n - 1} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle \langle u _ {n - 1}, u _ {n} \rangle + \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle \langle u _ {n}, u _ {n} \rangle \\ = \langle v, u _ {1} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {1} \rangle + \dots + \langle v, u _ {n} \rangle \langle v ^ {\prime}, u _ {n} \rangle . \\ \end{array}
$$

The above computation looks a little daunting, but only the linearity property of inner products and the fact that $\langle u_{i},u_{j}\rangle$ can equal either zero or one was used. Because inner products become dot products once one uses an orthonormal basis, we will quite often use the dot product notation in situations where one really should write an inner product. Conversely, dot product computations can always be rewritten in terms of an inner product, if needed.
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Example 133 Consider the space of polynomials given by $V=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\}$ with inner product $\langle p,p^{\prime}\rangle=\int_{0}^{1} p(x)p^{\prime}(x)dx.$ An obvious basis to use is B = (1,x) but it is not hard to check that this is not orthonormal, instead we take

$$
O = \left(1, 2 \sqrt {3} \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right)\right).
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
This is an orthonormal basis since,for example:

$$
\left\langle 2 \sqrt {3} \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right), 1 \right\rangle = 2 \sqrt {3} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right) d x = 0,
$$

and

$$
\left\langle x - \frac {1}{2}, x - \frac {1}{2} \right\rangle = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right) ^ {2} d x = \frac {1}{1 2} = \left(\frac {1}{2 \sqrt {3}}\right) ^ {2}.
$$

An arbitrary vector $v=a+b x$ is given in terms of the orthonormal basis O by

$$
v = \left(a + \frac {b}{2}\right). 1 + b \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right) = \left(1, 2 \sqrt {3} \left(x - \frac {1}{2}\right)\right) \binom {a + \frac {b}{2}} {\frac {b}{2 \sqrt {3}}} = \binom {a + \frac {b}{2}} {\frac {b}{2 \sqrt {3}}} _ {O}.
$$

Hence we can predict the inner product of $a+b x$ and $a^{\prime}+b^{\prime} x$ using the dot product:
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Hence we can predict the inner product of $a+b x$ and $a^{\prime}+b^{\prime} x$ using the dot product:

$$
\binom {a + \frac {b}{2}} {\frac {b}{2 \sqrt {3}}} \cdot \binom {a ^ {\prime} + \frac {b ^ {\prime}}{2}} {\frac {b ^ {\prime}}{2 \sqrt {3}}} = \left(a + \frac {b}{2}\right) \left(a ^ {\prime} + \frac {b ^ {\prime}}{2}\right) + \frac {b b ^ {\prime}}{1 2} = a a ^ {\prime} + \frac {1}{2} \left(a b ^ {\prime} + a ^ {\prime} b\right) + \frac {1}{3} b b ^ {\prime}.
$$

Indeed

$$
\langle a + b x, a ^ {\prime} + b ^ {\prime} x \rangle = \int_ {0} ^ {1} (a + b x) \left(a ^ {\prime} + b ^ {\prime} x\right) d x = a a ^ {\prime} + \frac {1}{2} \left(a b ^ {\prime} + a ^ {\prime} b\right) + \frac {1}{3} b b ^ {\prime}.
$$

## 14.3 Relating Orthonormal Bases

Suppose $T=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\}$ and $R=\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\}$ are two orthonormal bases for $\mathbb{R}^{n}.$ Then
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Suppose $T=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\}$ and $R=\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{n}\}$ are two orthonormal bases for $\mathbb{R}^{n}.$ Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} w _ {1} = \left(w _ {1} \cdot u _ {1}\right) u _ {1} + \dots + \left(w _ {1} \cdot u _ {n}\right) u _ {n} \\ \vdots \\ w _ {n} = \left(w _ {n} \cdot u _ {1}\right) u _ {1} + \dots + \left(w _ {n} \cdot u _ {n}\right) u _ {n} \\ \Rightarrow w _ {i} = \sum_ {j} u _ {j} \left(u _ {j} \cdot w _ {i}\right) \\ \end{array}
$$

Thus the matrix for the change of basis from $T$ to $R$ is given by

$$
P = \left(p _ {i} ^ {j}\right) = \left(u _ {j} \cdot w _ {i}\right).
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
We would like to calculate the product $P P^{T}$ . For that, we first develop a dirty trick for products of dot products:

$$
(u \cdot v) (w \cdot z) = \left(u ^ {T} v\right) \left(w ^ {T} z\right) = u ^ {T} \left(v w ^ {T}\right) z.
$$

The object $v w^{T}$ is the square matrix made from the outer product of $v$ and $w$ Now we are ready to compute the components of the matrix product $P P^{T}$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {i} \left(u _ {j} \cdot w _ {i}\right) \left(w _ {i} \cdot u _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {i} \left(u _ {j} ^ {T} w _ {i}\right) \left(w _ {i} ^ {T} u _ {k}\right) \\ = u _ {j} ^ {T} \left[ \sum_ {i} \left(w _ {i} w _ {i} ^ {T}\right) \right] u _ {k} \\ \stackrel {(*)} {=} u _ {j} ^ {T} I _ {n} u _ {k} \\ = u _ {j} ^ {T} u _ {k} = \delta_ {j k}. \\ \end{array}
$$

The equality (*) is explained below. Assuming (*) holds, we have shown that $P P^{T}=I_{n}$ , which implies that

$$
P ^ {T} = P ^ {- 1}.
$$

The equality in the line (*) says that $\sum_{i} w_{i} w_{i}^{T}=I_{n}.$ To see this, we examine $\left(\sum_{i} w_{i} w_{i}^{T}\right) v$ for an arbitrary vector $v.$ We can find constants $c^{j}$ such that $v=\sum_{i} c^{j} w_{j},$ so that
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(\sum_ {i} w _ {i} w _ {i} ^ {T}\right) v = \left(\sum_ {i} w _ {i} w _ {i} ^ {T}\right) \left(\sum_ {j} c ^ {j} w _ {j}\right) \\ = \sum_ {j} c ^ {j} \sum_ {i} w _ {i} w _ {i} ^ {T} w _ {j} \\ = \sum_ {j} c ^ {j} \sum_ {i} w _ {i} \delta_ {i j} \\ = \sum_ {j} c ^ {j} w _ {j} \mathrm {s i n c e a l t e r m s w i t h} i \neq j \mathrm {v a n i s h} \\ = v. \\ \end{array}
$$

Thus, as a linear transformation, $\sum_{i} w_{i} w_{i}^{T}=I_{n}$ fixes every vector, and thus must be the identity $I_{n}.$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Definition A matrix $P$ is orthogonal if $P^{-1} = P^{T}$.

Then to summarize,

Theorem 14.3.1. A change of basis matrix P relating two orthonormal bases is an orthogonal matrix. I.e.,

$$
P ^ {- 1} = P ^ {T}.
$$

Example 134 Consider $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with the ordered orthonormal basis

$$
S = \left(u _ {1}, u _ {2}, u _ {3}\right) = \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {2}{\sqrt {6}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {6}} \\ \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {6}} \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \end{array} \right)\right).
$$

Let E be the standard basis $( e_{1},e_{2},e_{3} )$ . Since we are changing from the standard basis to a new basis, then the columns of the change of basis matrix are exactly the new basis vectors. Then the change of basis matrix from E to S is given by
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
$$
\begin{array}{l} P = \left(P _ {i} ^ {j}\right) = \left(e _ {j} \cdot u _ {i}\right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} e _ {1} \cdot u _ {1} & e _ {1} \cdot u _ {2} & e _ {1} \cdot u _ {3} \\ e _ {2} \cdot u _ {1} & e _ {2} \cdot u _ {2} & e _ {2} \cdot u _ {3} \\ e _ {3} \cdot u _ {1} & e _ {3} \cdot u _ {2} & e _ {3} \cdot u _ {3} \end{array} \right) \\ = \left(u _ {1} u _ {2} u _ {3}\right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {2}{\sqrt {6}} & 0 & \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {6}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {3}} \\ \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {6}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$

From our theorem, we observe that
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
From our theorem, we observe that

$$
\begin{array}{l} P ^ {- 1} = P ^ {T} = \left( \begin{array}{c} u _ {1} ^ {T} \\ u _ {2} ^ {T} \\ u _ {3} ^ {T} \end{array} \right) \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {2}{\sqrt {6}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {6}} & \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {6}} \\ 0 & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} & \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {3}} & \frac {1}{\sqrt {3}} \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
We can check that $P^{T}P=I$ by a lengthy computation, or more simply, notice that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(P ^ {T} P\right) = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} u _ {1} ^ {T} \\ u _ {2} ^ {T} \\ u _ {3} ^ {T} \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} u _ {1} & u _ {2} & u _ {3} \end{array} \right) \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right). \\ \end{array}
$$

Above we are using orthonormality of the $u_{i}$ and the fact that matrix multiplication amounts to taking dot products between rows and columns. It is also very important to realize that the columns of an orthogonal matrix are made from an orthonormal set of vectors.

Orthonormal Change of Basis and Diagonal Matrices. Suppose D is a diagonal matrix and we are able to use an orthogonal matrix P to change to a new basis. Then the matrix M of D in the new basis is:

$$
M = P D P ^ {- 1} = P D P ^ {T}.
$$

Now we calculate the transpose of $M.$

$$
\begin{array}{l} M ^ {T} = \left(P D P ^ {T}\right) ^ {T} \\ = \left(P ^ {T}\right) ^ {T} D ^ {T} P ^ {T} \\ = P D P ^ {T} \\ = M \\ \end{array}
$$

The matrix $M=P D P^{T}$ is symmetric!

## 14.4 Gram-Schmidt & Orthogonal Complements

Given a vector v and some other vector u not in span $\{v\}$ we can construct the new vector

$$
v ^ {\perp} := v - \frac {u \cdot v}{u \cdot u} u.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
This new vector $v^{\perp}$ is orthogonal to u because

$$
u \cdot v ^ {\perp} = u \cdot v - \frac {u \cdot v}{u \cdot u} u \cdot u = 0.
$$

Hence, $\{u,v^{\perp}\}$ is an orthogonal basis for span $\{u,v\}$ . When v is not parallel to u, $v^{\perp}\neq0$ , and normalizing these vectors we obtain $\left\{\frac{u}{|u|},\frac{v^{\perp}}{|v^{\perp}|}\right\}$ , an orthonormal basis for the vector space span $\{u,v\}$ .

Sometimes we write $v=v^{\perp}+v^{\parallel}$ where:

$$
v ^ {\perp} = v - \frac {u \cdot v}{u \cdot u} u
$$

$$
v ^ {\parallel} = \frac {u \cdot v}{u \cdot u} u.
$$

This is called an orthogonal decomposition because we have decomposed $v$ into a sum of orthogonal vectors. This decomposition depends on u; if we change the direction of u we change $v^{\perp}$ and $v^{\parallel}.$

If $u, v$ are linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , then the set $\{u,v^{\perp},u\times v^{\perp}\}$ would be an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{3}.$ This set could then be normalized by dividing each vector by its length to obtain an orthonormal basis.

However, it often occurs that we are interested in vector spaces with dimension greater than 3, and must resort to craftier means than cross products to obtain an orthogonal basis $^{2}。$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
However, it often occurs that we are interested in vector spaces with dimension greater than 3, and must resort to craftier means than cross products to obtain an orthogonal basis $^{2}。$

$^{2}$ Actually, given a set T of (n-1) independent vectors in n-space, one can define an analogue of the cross product that will produce a vector orthogonal to the span of T, using a method exactly analogous to the usual computation for calculating the cross product of two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . This only gets us the "last" orthogonal vector, though; the Gram-Schmidt process described in this section gives a way to get a full orthogonal basis.
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Given a third vector w, we should first check that w does not lie in the span $\{u,v\}$ , i.e., check that u, v and w are linearly independent. If it does not, we then can define

$$
w ^ {\perp} := w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} u - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} v ^ {\perp}.
$$

We can check that $u \cdot w^{\perp}$ and $v^{\perp}\cdot w^{\perp}$ are both zero:

$$
\begin{array}{l} u \cdot w ^ {\perp} = u \cdot \left(w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} u - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} v ^ {\perp}\right) \\ = u \cdot w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} u \cdot u - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} u \cdot v ^ {\perp} \\ = u \cdot w - u \cdot w - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} u \cdot v ^ {\perp} = 0 \\ \end{array}
$$

since u is orthogonal to $v^{\perp}$ , and
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
since u is orthogonal to $v^{\perp}$ , and

$$
\begin{array}{l} v ^ {\perp} \cdot w ^ {\perp} = v ^ {\perp} \cdot \left(w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} u - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} v ^ {\perp}\right) \\ = v ^ {\perp} \cdot w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} v ^ {\perp} \cdot u - \frac {v ^ {\perp} \cdot w}{v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp}} v ^ {\perp} \cdot v ^ {\perp} \\ = v ^ {\perp} \cdot w - \frac {u \cdot w}{u \cdot u} v ^ {\perp} \cdot u - v ^ {\perp} \cdot w = 0 \\ \end{array}
$$

because u is orthogonal to $v^{\perp}$ . Since $w^{\perp}$ is orthogonal to both u and $v^{\perp}$ , we have that $\{u,v^{\perp},w^{\perp}\}$ is an orthogonal basis for span $\{u,v,w\}$ .
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
## 14.4.1 The Gram-Schmidt Procedure

In fact, given an ordered set $(v_{1}, v_{2}, \dots)$ of linearly independent vectors, we can define an orthogonal basis for span $\{v_{1}, v_{2}, \dots\}$ consisting of the vectors

$$
\begin{array}{l} v _ {1} ^ {\perp} := v _ {1} \\ v _ {2} ^ {\perp} := v _ {2} - \frac {v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {2}}{v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {1} ^ {\perp}} v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \\ v _ {3} ^ {\perp} := v _ {3} - \frac {v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {3}}{v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {1} ^ {\perp}} v _ {1} ^ {\perp} - \frac {v _ {2} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {3}}{v _ {2} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {2} ^ {\perp}} v _ {2} ^ {\perp} \\ \vdots \\ v _ {i} ^ {\perp} := v _ {i} - \frac {v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {i}}{v _ {1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {1} ^ {\perp}} v _ {1} ^ {\perp} - \frac {v _ {2} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {i}}{v _ {2} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {2} ^ {\perp}} v _ {2} ^ {\perp} - \dots - \frac {v _ {i - 1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {i}}{v _ {i - 1} ^ {\perp} \cdot v _ {i - 1} ^ {\perp}} v _ {i - 1} ^ {\perp} \\ \vdots \\ \end{array}
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Notice that each $v_{i}^{\perp}$ here depends on $v_{j}^{\perp}$ for every j<i. This allows us to inductively/algorithmically build up a linearly independent, orthogonal set of vectors $\{v_{1}^{\perp}, v_{2}^{\perp},\ldots\}$ such that span $\{v_{1}^{\perp}, v_{2}^{\perp},\ldots\} = \operatorname{span}\{v_{1}, v_{2},\ldots\}$ . That is, an orthogonal basis for the latter vector space.

Note that the set of vectors you start out with needs to be ordered to uniquely specify the algorithm; changing the order of the vectors will give a different orthogonal basis. You might need to be the one to put an order on the initial set of vectors.

This algorithm is called the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure-Gram worked at a Danish insurance company over one hundred years ago, Schmidt was a student of Hilbert (the famous German mathmatician).

Example 135 We'll obtain an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ by appling Gram-Schmidt to the linearly independent set $\left\{\left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right),\left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right),\left( \begin{array}{c} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) \right\}.$

Because he Gram-Schmidt algorithm uses the first vector from the ordered set the largest number of times, we will choose the vector with the most zeros to be the first in hopes of simplifying computations; we choose to order the set as

$$
(v _ {1}, v _ {2}, v _ {3}) := \left(\left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right)\right).
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
First, we set $v_{1}^{\perp} \coloneqq v_{1}.$ Then

$$
v _ {2} ^ {\perp} := \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) - \frac {2}{2} \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right)
$$

$$
v _ {3} ^ {\perp} := \left( \begin{array}{c} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) - \frac {4}{2} \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right) - \frac {1}{1} \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ - 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right).
$$

Then the set

$$
\left\{\left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ - 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right) \right\}
$$

is an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . To obtain an orthonormal basis we simply divide each of these vectors by its length, yielding

\left\{\left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ \frac {- 1}{\sqrt {2}} \\ 0 \end{array} \right) \right\}.

## 14.5 QR Decomposition

In Chapter 7, Section 7.7 teaches you how to solve linear systems by decomposing a matrix M into a product of lower and upper triangular matrices

$$
M = L U.
$$

The Gram-Schmidt procedure suggests another matrix decomposition,

$$
M = Q R,
$$

where Q is an orthogonal matrix and R is an upper triangular matrix. So-called QR-decompositions are useful for solving linear systems, eigenvalue problems and least squares approximations. You can easily get the idea behind the QR decomposition by working through a simple example.
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Example 136 Find the QR decomposition of

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 2 & - 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & - 2 \\ 0 & 1 & - 2 \end{array} \right).
$$

What we will do is to think of the columns of M as three 3-vectors and use Gram-Schmidt to build an orthonormal basis from these that will become the columns of the orthogonal matrix Q. We will use the matrix R to record the steps of the Gram-Schmidt procedure in such a way that the product QR equals M.

To begin with we write

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 2 & - \frac {7}{5} & 1 \\ 1 & \frac {1 4}{5} & - 2 \\ 0 & 1 & - 2 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & \frac {1}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right).
$$

In the first matrix the first two columns are orthogonal because we simply replaced the second column of M by the vector that the Gram-Schmidt procedure produces from the first two columns of M, namely

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c} - \frac {7}{5} \\ \frac {1 4}{5} \\ 1 \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} - 1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array} \right) - \frac {1}{5} \left( \begin{array}{c} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right).
$$

The matrix on the right is almost the identity matrix, save the $+\frac{1}{5}$ in the second entry of the first row, whose effect upon multiplying the two matrices precisely undoes what we we did to the second column of the first matrix.

For the third column of M we use Gram-Schmidt to deduce the third orthogonal vector
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
For the third column of M we use Gram-Schmidt to deduce the third orthogonal vector

$$
\left( \begin{array}{c} - \frac {1}{6} \\ \frac {1}{3} \\ - \frac {7}{6} \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ - 2 \\ - 2 \end{array} \right) - 0 \left( \begin{array}{c} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right) - \frac {- 9}{\frac {5 4}{5}} \left( \begin{array}{c} - \frac {7}{5} \\ \frac {1 4}{5} \\ 1 \end{array} \right),
$$

and therefore, using exactly the same procedure write

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 2 & - \frac {7}{5} & - \frac {1}{6} \\ 1 & \frac {1 4}{5} & \frac {1}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & - \frac {7}{6} \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & \frac {1}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - \frac {5}{6} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right).
$$

This is not quite the answer because the first matrix is now made of mutually orthogonal column vectors, but a bona fide orthogonal matrix is comprised of orthonormal
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
vectors. To achieve that we divide each column of the first matrix by its length and multiply the corresponding row of the second matrix by the same amount:

$$
M = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \frac {2 \sqrt {5}}{5} & - \frac {7 \sqrt {3 0}}{9 0} & - \frac {\sqrt {6}}{1 8} \\ \frac {\sqrt {5}}{5} & \frac {7 \sqrt {3 0}}{4 5} & \frac {\sqrt {6}}{9} \\ 0 & \frac {\sqrt {3 0}}{1 8} & - \frac {7 \sqrt {6}}{1 8} \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c c} \sqrt {5} & \frac {\sqrt {5}}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac {3 \sqrt {3 0}}{5} & - \frac {\sqrt {3 0}}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \frac {\sqrt {6}}{2} \end{array} \right) = Q R.
$$

Geometrically what has happened here is easy to see. We started with three vectors given by the columns of M and rotated them such that the first lies along the x-axis, the second in the xy-plane and the third in some other generic direction (here it happens to be in the yz-plane).

A nice check of the above result is to verify that entry $(i,j)$ of the matrix R equals the dot product of the i-th column of Q with the j-th column of M. (Some people memorize this fact and use it as a recipe for computing QR decompositions.) A good test of your own understanding is to work out why this is true!

## 14.6 Orthogonal Complements

Let U and V be subspaces of a vector space W. In Review Exercise 2, Chapter 9, you are asked to show that $U \cap V$ is a subspace of W, and that $U \cup V$ is not a subspace. However, $\operatorname{span}(U \cup V)$ is certainly a subspace, since the span of any subset of a vector space is a subspace. Notice that all elements of $\operatorname{span}(U \cup V)$ take the form u+v with u $\in U$ and v $\in V.$ We call the subspace

$$
U + V := \operatorname {s p a n} (U \cup V) = \{u + v \mid u \in U, v \in V\}
$$

the sum of U and V. Here, we are not adding vectors, but vector spaces to produce a new vector space.

Example 137

$$
\operatorname {s p a n} \left\{\left( \begin{array}{l l l} 1 & \\ 1 & \\ 0 & \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{l l l} 0 & \\ 1 & \\ 1 & \\ 0 \end{array} \right) \right\} + \operatorname {s p a n} \left\{\left( \begin{array}{l l l} 0 & \\ 1 & \\ 1 & \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{l l l} 0 & \\ 0 & \\ 1 & \\ 1 \end{array} \right) \right\} = \operatorname {s p a n} \left\{\left( \begin{array}{l l l} 1 & \\ 1 & \\ 0 & \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{l l l} 0 & \\ 1 & \\ 1 & \\ 0 \end{array} \right), \left( \begin{array}{l l l} 0 & \\ 0 & \\ 1 & \\ 1 \end{array} \right) \right\}.
$$
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
Notice that the addends have elements in common; $\left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right)$ is in both addends. Even though both of the addends are 2-dimensional their sum is not 4-dimensional.

In the special case that U and V do not have any non-zero vectors in common, their sum is a vector space with dimension $\dim U+\dim V.$

Definition If U and V are subspaces of a vector space W such that $U\cap V=\{0_{W}\}$ then the vector space

$$
U \oplus V := \operatorname {s p a n} (U \cup V) = \{u + v \mid u \in U, v \in V \}
$$

is the direct sum of U and V.

## Remark

- When $U \cap V=\{0_{W}\}$ $U+V=U\oplus V.$

This distinction is important because the direct sum has a very nice property:

Theorem 14.6.1. If $w \in U\oplus V$ then there is only one way to write w as the sum of a vector in U and a vector in V.

Suppose that $u+v=u^{\prime}+v^{\prime}$ with $u,u^{\prime}\in U$ and $v,v^{\prime}\in V$ . Then we could express 0 $=(u-u^{\prime})+(v-v^{\prime})$ . Then $( u-u^{\prime} )=-( v-v^{\prime} )$ . Since U and V are subspaces, we have $( u-u^{\prime} )\in U$ and $-( v-v^{\prime} )\in V$ . But since these elements are equal, we also have $( u-u^{\prime} )\in V$ . Since $U \cap V=\{0\}$ , then $( u-u^{\prime})=0$ . Similarly, $( v-v^{\prime} )=0$ . Therefore $u=u^{\prime}$ and $v=v^{\prime}$ , proving the theorem.

## Reading homework: problem 3

Here is a sophisticated algebra question:

Given a subspace U in W, what are the solutions to

$$
U \oplus V = W.
$$

That is, how can we write W as the direct sum of U and something?
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
There is not a unique answer to this question as can be seen from the following picture of subspaces in $W=\mathbb{R}^{3}.$

However, using the inner product, there is a natural candidate $U^{\perp}$ for this second subspace as shown below.

Definition If U is a subspace of the vector space W then the vector space

$$
U ^ {\perp} := \left\{w \in W \mid w \cdot u = 0 \text {f o r a l l} u \in U \right\}
$$

is the orthogonal complement of U in W.

Remark The symbols $" U^{\perp} "$ are often read as $" U-$ perp". This is the set of all vectors in W orthogonal to every vector in U. Notice also that in the above definition we have implicitly assumed that the inner product is the dot product. For a general inner product, the above definition would read $U^{\perp} := \left\{ w \in W \mid \langle w, u \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } u \in U \right\}$

text:
Possibly by now you are feeling overwhelmed, it may help to watch this quick overview video.

Overview

Example 138 Consider any plane P through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^{3}.$ Then P is a subspace, and $P^{\perp}$ is the line through the origin orthogonal to P. For example, if P is the xy-plane, then

$$
\mathbb {R} ^ {3} = P \oplus P ^ {\perp} = \{(x, y, 0) | x, y \in \mathbb {R} \} \oplus \{(0, 0, z) | z \in \mathbb {R} \}.
$$

Theorem 14.6.2. Let U be a subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space W. Then the set $U^{\perp}$ is a subspace of W, and $W=U\oplus U^{\perp}.$

Proof. First, to see that $U^{\perp}$ is a subspace, we only need to check closure which requires a simple check: Suppose v,w $\in U^{\perp}$ , then we know

$$
v \cdot u = 0 = w \cdot u \quad (\forall u \in U).
$$

Hence

$$
\Rightarrow u \cdot (\alpha v + \beta w) = \alpha u \cdot v + \beta u \cdot w = 0 \quad (\forall u \in U),
$$

$\alpha v+\beta w\in U^{\perp}.$

Next, to form a direct sum between U and $U^{\perp}$ we need to show that $U \cap U^{\perp}=\{0\}$ . This holds because if $u\in U$ and $u\in U^{\perp}$ it follows that

$$
u \cdot u = 0 \Leftrightarrow u = 0.
$$

Finally, we show that any vector $w\in W$ is in $U\oplus U^{\perp}$ . (This is where we use the assumption that W is finite-dimensional.) Let $e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}$ be an orthonormal basis for U. Set:
title: What is Linear Algebra?

text:
$$
\begin{array}{l} u = \left(w \cdot e _ {1}\right) e _ {1} + \dots + \left(w \cdot e _ {n}\right) e _ {n} \in U, \\ u ^ {\perp} = w - u. \\ \end{array}
$$

It is easy to check that $u^{\perp}\in U^{\perp}$ (see the Gram-Schmidt procedure). Then $w=u+u^{\perp}$ , so $w\in U\oplus U^{\perp}$ , and we are done.
